## 119e. The Interstellar Visitors — 3I/ATLAS and the Family of Wanderers [SOLVED as class / 'Oumuamua CONTESTED]

In the nine years since 'Oumuamua tumbled through the inner solar system, three confirmed interstellar objects have been discovered — 1I/'Oumuamua (2017), 2I/Borisov (2019), and 3I/ATLAS (2025) — and each has rewritten in real time what we know about the planetary systems of other stars.

3I/ATLAS is the richest of the three. Discovered by the ATLAS survey on July 1, 2025, at 4.5 AU inbound, it was intercepted by virtually every major observatory and spacecraft: Hubble, Webb, SPHEREx, TESS, Swift, SOHO, the Perseverance rover and two orbiters at Mars, and the en-route Europa Clipper, Lucy, Psyche, Parker Solar Probe, and Juice — a nineteen-spacecraft campaign unprecedented in solar system history. Its nucleus is small — under 5.6 km, possibly as small as 440 meters — but its chemistry is extraordinary. JWST found a CO2-dominated coma, enhanced in both CO2 and CO relative to water compared to typical solar system comets; isotopic evidence points to formation in a cold, distant part of another protoplanetary disk. SPHEREx detected organic molecules — methanol, cyanide, methane, water, soot, and rock dust — venting from subsurface ice that had been sealed beneath a cosmic-ray-processed crust for billions of years, and observed the comet brighten sharply two months after perihelion as solar heat finally penetrated the radiation-hardened shell. ALMA mapped CH3OH and HCN in the coma and found a remarkably high methanol-to-HCN ratio. Nickel and iron emission appeared at unusually large heliocentric distances. The picture that emerged: a planetesimal forged in the outer, cold periphery of a relatively calm planetary system, bearing material unchanged since before our Sun's planets formed. When it departed past Jupiter in mid-2026, every telescope on Earth and in space had learned more from one interstellar grain of sand than from centuries of looking outward. The Loeb-adjacent speculation that briefly flared in 2025 is logged with the CNEOS1 entry (Section 119d): natural, cometary, and solved.

'Oumuamua (2017) remains the contested one. Its anomaly was never its shape but its exit: as it left the inner solar system, it carried a small, sun-directed non-gravitational acceleration (Micheli et al., Nature, 2018) with no coma, no tail, and no detected outgassing — a force without a visible cause. The natural explanations now form a queue: the 2021 nitrogen-iceberg hypothesis (Desch & Jackson — a chip off an exo-Pluto), the 2023 hydrogen-entrapment model (Bergner & Seligman, Nature: cosmic-ray-processed water ice releasing trapped H2 as it warms, producing a dust-free push, with the required high area-to-mass ratio naturally explaining the disk-like light curve), and the 2023 PNAS "dark comet" follow-up identifying near-Earth asteroids with the same invisible-push signature, proving the phenomenon class exists. The Bern group's laboratory critique (Ligterink et al., 2023) showed the hydrogen yield requires an implausibly old, implausibly water-rich body, keeping the question genuinely open. Loeb's light-sail hypothesis (Bialy & Loeb 2018) was answered institutionally: the fourteen-member ISSI consensus review, "The Natural History of 'Oumuamua" (Nature Astronomy, 2019), found every observation consistent with a natural, if unusual, icy body. The object is now beyond every telescope; the verdict of the instruments stands: anomalous natural, with two independent mechanisms on file, and an artificial reading that survives only outside the literature.

2I/Borisov (2019) was the ordinary one that proved the extraordinary: a textbook comet from another star, red, carbon-rich, with the highest CO abundance ratio ever measured in any comet — and the first proof that other solar systems make comets the way ours does. Together the three visitors frame the anomaly's final form: interstellar objects pass through constantly (the discovery rate implies a population in the trillions), every one of them is a free sample of another world's construction material, and only the first one ever seen refuses, so far, to be fully explained.

# PART XIII — FRINGE CLAIMS, DOCUMENTED

## 120. Bigfoot, Nessie, and the DNA Record [CONTESTED → DEBUNKED]

The cryptozoological canon — Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, the Yeti — has been tested by the one instrument that cannot be argued with: DNA. The results are uniform and, for the believers, devastating.

**Sykes's 2013–2014 study.** Oxford geneticist Bryan Sykes, working with the Lausanne Museum of Zoology, solicited hair and tissue samples from 37 claimed anomalous primates — Bigfoot, Yeti, Almasty, orang pendek, and others — and subjected them to mitochondrial DNA analysis. The results: all but two matched known mammals (bears, dogs, cows, raccoons, deer, and, memorably, a porcupine). Two samples — from Ladakh and Bhutan, attributed to the Yeti — matched a polar bear jawbone from Svalbard dating to 40,000 years ago, suggesting a previously unknown hybrid or relict polar-bear population in the Himalayas. The finding made headlines as the "Yeti bear." The correction came in 2015: Edwards and Barnett showed the Svalbard jawbone had been misidentified; it was a modern polar bear of the Diomede population, and the "unknown hybrid" vanished. Sykes conceded the error. The cryptozoological residue: two samples of uncertain identity in a dataset of 37, both likely bears.

**The Ketchum study.** In 2013, veterinarian Melba Ketchum announced a five-year study of 111 Bigfoot DNA samples, claiming to have identified a novel hominin — a hybrid of *Homo sapiens* and an unknown primate — with a full mitochondrial genome sequence and nuclear DNA from hair, blood, and tissue. The study was self-published in a journal (the *DeNovo Journal of Science*) that Ketchum had purchased specifically for the purpose after mainstream journals rejected it; the "novel haplotypes" were shown by subsequent analysis to be consistent with known human contamination and laboratory artifacts; the journal ceased publication. The claim is preserved here as the canonical example of credential-mimicking science: real laboratory techniques, real data, wrong conclusion, no replication.

**Loch Ness eDNA (2019).** Neil Gemmell's team from the University of Otago sampled water from every corner of Loch Ness, extracting environmental DNA — the genetic fragments all organisms shed into their surroundings — and catalogued every species present. The results: no reptile DNA (ruling out plesiosaurs, the favored Nessie candidate); no sturgeon; no catfish. The fish community was exactly as expected for a Scottish loch. About 25 percent of the sequences were unidentifiable, but the same proportion of unidentifiable sequences appeared in the control lochs — the "unknowns" are sequencing artifacts, not monsters. The one finding that made headlines: a significant population of European eels, large enough that a very large eel cannot be ruled out as the source of some sightings. Gemmell's conclusion: "There may be giant eels in Loch Ness. We don't know — but we can't rule it out." It is the most generous result the DNA evidence allows.

The pattern across all three cases is identical: the physical evidence, when it exists, is always a known species, a laboratory artifact, or a hoax. The sightings, footprints, and photographs continue — hundreds per year for Bigfoot alone — but the DNA record is empty. The anomaly, resolved: the cryptids are not hiding from the instruments. They are not there to be found.


## 120a. Loch Ness eDNA — the Genetic Census [SOLVED as inventory / residue preserved]

The most rigorous scientific test ever applied to the Loch Ness monster hypothesis came not from a submarine or a sonar sweep but from a liter of water. In 2018–2019, Neil Gemmell, a geneticist at the University of Otago, led an international team that collected 250 water samples from every corner of the loch — from the surface to within meters of the 230-meter bottom, from the open water to the river mouths, from the main basin to the connected lochs of the Great Glen. The method was environmental DNA (eDNA): every organism in the loch sheds fragments of DNA into the water — skin cells, scales, feces, urine — and those fragments can be captured, sequenced, and matched against global genetic databases to produce a complete census of everything living in the water.

The results, published in September 2019, were the most comprehensive biological survey of Loch Ness ever conducted. The team identified all 13 fish species known to live in the loch. They identified frogs, toads, ducks, deer, badgers, foxes, rabbits, voles, sheep, cattle, dogs, and humans — the land-based DNA reflecting the steep-sided mountains that funnel terrestrial genetic material into the water. They identified a microbiome of bacteria, fungi, and salt-loving archaea. And they found no reptile DNA of any kind, no shark DNA, no catfish DNA, no sturgeon DNA, and nothing else that would qualify as a large unknown animal. The plesiosaur hypothesis — the most famous and most persistent of the Nessie theories — was explicitly excluded: "We can't find any evidence of a creature that's remotely related to that in our environmental-DNA sequence data."

The one residue that survived the survey was eels. The loch has a significant population of European eels (*Anguilla anguilla*), which enter as larvae from the Sargasso Sea, grow in the loch for years, and would normally return to the ocean to spawn. The eDNA could not distinguish between ordinary and giant individuals, and Gemmell was careful to state the limitation: "There is a very significant amount of eel DNA. Eels are very plentiful in Loch Ness, with eel DNA found at pretty much every location sampled... So — are they giant eels? Well, our data doesn't reveal their size, but the sheer quantity of the material says that we can't discount the possibility that there may be giant eels in Loch Ness."

The giant eel hypothesis has a specific and checkable logic. European eels grow throughout their lives and do not return to spawn if they cannot reach the sea. In a closed freshwater system, an eel that misses its migratory window could, in principle, grow to an unusual size. Divers have reported eels "as thick as their legs" in the loch. A four-meter eel — the size implied by some surface sightings — would be exceptional but not biologically impossible. Gemmell's own assessment: "While an eel that big would be well outside the normal range, it seems not impossible that something could grow to such unusual size." The hypothesis survives the eDNA test because the test cannot measure size. Every other hypothesis — plesiosaur, sturgeon, catfish, shark, seal, otter, floating log, boat wake, bird raft, and the rest of the catalogue — either fails the DNA test or fails the physical evidence.

The 2019 study's most important finding was not about the monster at all. It established a comprehensive, publicly accessible genetic database for Loch Ness — a baseline against which any future biological change in the loch can be measured. eDNA is now the standard tool for monitoring freshwater ecosystems worldwide, and the Loch Ness project demonstrated its power on the world's most famous body of water. The monster search produced a biodiversity map.

The anomaly, precisely stated: the largest body of fresh water in the British Isles, one of the most intensively observed bodies of water on Earth, has been genetically surveyed at every depth and every corner. The inventory is complete. The one thing the survey cannot rule out is a large eel. Everything else — every theory that requires an unknown species, a prehistoric survivor, or a creature outside the known taxonomy of the British Isles — is excluded by the data. The loch has been read, letter by letter, and the only word it will not surrender is "eel."

## 121. Mothman and the Mad Gasser [SOLVED as phenomena]

Two of America's most famous monster flaps are preserved here together, because both dissolved under the same examination — ordinary psychology under extraordinary stress, amplified by the media ecology of its era.

**Mothman (Point Pleasant, West Virginia, 1966–67).** From November 1966, residents of Point Pleasant reported a large grey figure, seven feet tall, with enormous wings and two glowing red eyes — seen on roadsides, on rooftops, in the TNT area's abandoned munitions bunkers. The sightings ran for thirteen months and ended with a catastrophe: on December 15, 1967, the Silver Bridge connecting Point Pleasant to Ohio collapsed during rush hour, killing forty-six people. The linkage, cemented by John Keel's 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies and the 2002 film, presents Mothman as a herald — the omen that warned of the bridge. The record, read closely, offers no omen. The sightings cluster near the TNT area, which held breeding colonies of the large birds most capable of generating the reports: the sandhill crane, which stands five feet tall, is grey, has reddish eye-shine at night, and was uncommon enough in West Virginia to be unfamiliar to its observers; and the barred owl, whose large dark eyes reflect light as burning red, and whose deep forest habitat matches the sighting locations. An escaped aviary specimen — a large bird reared by a local eccentric, released or escaped in late 1966 — would fit the timeline exactly. The NTSB's verdict on the bridge was mundane and specific: a single eyebar, corroded for years, suffered a stress-corrosion crack and failed; the bridge was structurally deficient, overloaded, and forty years old. Mothman was a bird; the bridge was a machine at the end of its life. The two events were adjacent in space and time, not causally linked — and the human need to bind a catastrophe to a warning is the only real anomaly the case contains.

**The Mad Gasser of Mattoon (Illinois, 1944).** Over two weeks in August and September 1944, residents of Mattoon reported a prowler who sprayed paralyzing gas into bedroom windows, leaving victims nauseated and partially paralyzed. The Anesthetic Prowler, as the papers also called him, was never caught, seen clearly by no one, and left no physical trace — no gas residue, no footprints in soft ground, no chemical signature. Johnson's 1945 analysis, the founding study of mass hysteria, examined every report and found the classic signature: symptoms spread faster than any plausible poison could travel, victims recovered with implausible speed, the prowler's description shifted with each telling, and the incidents crested and died with newspaper coverage — when the papers stopped printing, the Gasser stopped gassing. The episode is now a textbook case of mass psychogenic illness: a community under wartime stress, primed by lurid headlines, generating symptoms through anxiety and suggestion. Both cases document the same manufacturing process: an ambiguous stimulus, a frightened community, a press engine, and a mythology assembled in real time. The monsters were real — as experiences. Their reality ended at the skin.


## 122a. The Dogon Sirius B Controversy — a Mystery That Wasn't [DEBUNKED — contamination by ethnographer / source documented]

In 1931, the French anthropologist Marcel Griaule arrived in the Bandiagara Escarpment of what is now Mali to study the Dogon people, an agricultural society of approximately 400,000 people who had maintained their traditional culture despite centuries of contact with Islam and European colonialism. Griaule spent decades among the Dogon, developing a reputation as one of the most brilliant and innovative ethnographers of his generation. His methods were groundbreaking: he used aerial photography, systematic surveys, and team-based research. His findings about Dogon cosmology — published in *Conversations with Ogotemmeli* (1948) and *The Pale Fox* (1965, co-authored with Germaine Dieterlen) — were extraordinary. They were also, in their most famous claim, almost certainly wrong.

The claim was this: the Dogon possessed ancient, pre-colonial knowledge of Sirius B — the white dwarf companion of Sirius A, a star invisible to the naked eye, discovered by Western astronomers in 1862 and confirmed spectroscopically in 1915. Griaule reported that the Dogon knew not only of Sirius B's existence but also its orbital period (50 years, which they said was counted as 100 years due to the Dogon principle of "twinness"), its extreme density (they reportedly said that a piece of it the size of a grain of millet would weigh as much as all the iron on Earth), and its elliptical orbit around Sirius A. The source of this knowledge, Griaule reported, was the Nommo — amphibious ancestral spirits who had come from the Sirius system and taught the Dogon their cosmology. The implication was staggering: either the Dogon had independently discovered astronomical facts that required telescopes and spectroscopes to confirm, or they had preserved knowledge given to them by extraterrestrial visitors.

The claim entered the public consciousness through Robert Temple's 1976 book *The Sirius Mystery*, which argued that the Dogon's knowledge could only be explained by ancient extraterrestrial contact — a hypothesis that became a cornerstone of the ancient astronaut genre. Carl Sagan, in *Broca's Brain* (1979), noted the simpler explanation: the Dogon could have learned about Sirius B from European visitors (missionaries, colonial administrators, or astronomers) who knew of its 1862 discovery and subsequent characterization. Ian Ridpath, in a 1978 *Skeptical Inquirer* article, documented the inconsistencies, contradictions, and errors in Griaule's account, concluding that the Dogon legend was "riddled with ambiguities, contradictions, and downright errors" and that any resemblance to actual facts about Sirius was likely the result of cultural contact with Europeans.

The decisive blow came in 1991. Walter van Beek, a Dutch anthropologist who had spent seven years among the Dogon, published "Dogon Restudied: A Field Evaluation of the Work of Marcel Griaule" in *Current Anthropology*. Van Beek attempted to replicate Griaule's findings by interviewing Dogon elders about Sirius and the Nommo. His findings were devastating. The Dogon he interviewed did not know that Sirius was a double star. They did not agree on which star "Sigu Tolo" (the star Griaule identified as Sirius) even was — some identified it as Venus, others as an invisible star that announced the Sigu festival, others as a star they had learned about from Griaule himself. Most damningly, several Dogon told van Beek explicitly that they had learned about Sirius from Griaule — that the anthropologist had told them about the star and its companion, and that they had incorporated this information into their responses to his questions. The "ancient knowledge" was not ancient. It was contamination — information introduced by the researcher himself, fed back to him by informants who were trying to please the powerful colonial authority figure with the pith helmet and the notebook.

The methodological critique is comprehensive. Griaule's primary informant was a single blind hunter named Ogotemmeli, who was not necessarily the most authoritative source for Dogon cosmology. Griaule worked through an interpreter, raising the possibility of translation errors. He never published the raw transcripts of his interviews, making it impossible to verify whether his interpretations matched what his informants actually said. He had a demonstrated tendency to systematize — to impose a Western philosophical framework on Dogon thought, creating elaborate cosmological structures (cosmic eggs, mystic vibrations, the Nommo mythology) that bore little resemblance to the simpler, more practical beliefs that van Beek found in his restudy. The "courtesy bias" — the tendency of informants to tell the researcher what they think he wants to hear — was documented by van Beek as a systematic distortion in Griaule's work. Griaule was not a fraud; he was a brilliant, imaginative scholar whose enthusiasm for the complexity of Dogon cosmology led him to see more structure and more knowledge than was actually there.

The 1995 Benest and Duvent study added a footnote: the possibility of a third star in the Sirius system (Sirius C) could not be ruled out based on anomalous perturbations of Sirius B. This finding was seized upon by believers as confirmation of the Dogon's claim that Sirius had three components (Sirius A, B, and the hypothetical "Emme Ya"). However, the 1973 Lindenblad observations showed no evidence of a close companion to either Sirius A or B, and subsequent studies have found no Sirius C. The claim remains [FRINGE-CLAIM].

The Dogon Sirius B controversy is preserved in this document as the canonical case study in how not to do anthropology — and how not to evaluate extraordinary claims. The chain of failure is instructive: a single informant, working through an interpreter, telling a researcher what he wants to hear; a researcher who systematizes and elaborates; a popularizer (Temple) who amplifies the most extraordinary interpretation; a public that prefers aliens to Occam's Razor; and a restudy (van Beek) that takes decades to correct the record. The Sirius Mystery sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Van Beek's "Dogon Restudied" is read by specialists. The correction never caught up with the myth.

The anomaly is not that the Dogon knew about Sirius B. They didn't. The anomaly is that the story was believed for so long — by scientists, by the media, by the public — despite the evidence being available from the start. Griaule's own data contained the seeds of the debunking: the 50-year orbital period was described as 100 years (explained by "twinness"), the "invisible star" was variously identified as Venus or as a star that announced a festival, and the density claim was expressed in metaphorical terms that could describe almost anything heavy. The debunking required only someone to go back and ask the Dogon what they actually believed. It took 40 years for someone to do that. The Sirius Mystery was not a mystery. It was a mirror — reflecting what the researchers and their audience wanted to see, not what was there.

## 122. Ancient Astronauts and the Forbidden-Archaeology Corpus [FRINGE-CLAIM]

The ancient-astronaut hypothesis — that extraterrestrial visitors engineered human civilization, built the monuments, and seeded the myths — is the twentieth century's most industrious pseudohistory, and its anatomy is worth preserving in full, because every mechanism by which it persuades is a distortion of a real method. The corpus descends from Erich von Däniken's Chariots of the Gods? (1968), which sold tens of millions of copies and established the genre's formula: find an ancient artifact that looks technically anomalous, declare it beyond the builders' ability, and assign it to visitors from space. The case studies collapse under examination one by one. The Nazca Lines (Section 44) are processional paths, made by walkers, not runways — no landing strip requires a kilometer of shallow trench removed from desert pavement, and the aliens who crossed interstellar space are presumed, without argument, to need 2,000-year-old Peruvian ground crews. The Baalbek trilithon (Section 31) is moved by documented Roman technique. The Great Pyramid's casing stones (Section 47) were quarried, not cast. The Piri Reis map (Section 108) is an Ottoman compilation, its "accuracy" reconstructed by modern believers through selective projection. Every single "impossible artifact" in the canon, when examined by specialists with access to the actual object, turns out to be either a natural formation, a misdated artifact, or a hoax — the Coso artifact, the London Hammer, the crystal skulls, all catalogued in Section 107.

The genre's successor is the "forbidden archaeology" movement, whose foundational text — Michael Cremo and Richard Thompson's Forbidden Archeology (1993) — argues that mainstream science suppresses evidence of extreme human antiquity. The suppression claim fails on its face: the reward structure of science runs entirely the other way. A genuine out-of-place fossil or anomalous artifact would make its finder's career instantly and permanently; Nature and Science would compete to publish it; the discoverer of a 250-million-year-old human footprint would dine out on it for the rest of their life. That this has never happened is not evidence of conspiracy. It is evidence that the artifacts, examined, are not what the fringe claims — the Klerksdorp spheres are natural concretions, the Meister print is a spall fracture, the Saqqara Bird is a falcon with a missing tail feather.

The legitimate point the fringe gets right — that orthodox science has been wrong before, and that the history of science is full of anomalies dismissed prematurely — is preserved here and granted fully. Quasicrystals were "impossible" until they weren't. Ball lightning was hallucination until it wasn't. The deep biosphere was absurd until it wasn't. That is precisely why this document exists: because some anomalies are real. But the difference between the anomaly that survives and the anomaly that dissolves is never the enthusiasm of its believers. It is what happens when someone looks at it directly. The ancient-astronaut corpus has been looked at directly, by archaeologists, engineers, and historians, for sixty years. What survives examination is the monuments — magnificent, human, and ours. What dissolves is the visitors, who were never needed, never evidenced, and never there. The stars were always far away. The ancestors were always enough.


## 123. EVP and the Stone Tape [FRINGE-CLAIM / SOLVED as folklore]

Electronic Voice Phenomena — the voices heard in static, in tape hiss, in the noise floor of any recording — are among the most persistent of the ghost-hunter's tools, and the most completely explained. The mechanism is auditory pareidolia: the brain's pattern-completion machinery, evolved to extract speech from the most degraded acoustic environments, imposes words and voices on random noise with the same force that it imposes faces on cloud formations and toast. The effect is powerful, universal, and irrepressible — knowing the mechanism does not disable it, which is why even skeptical researchers continue to "hear" the words their colleagues point out. The ghost boxes and "spirit radios" marketed to investigators remove even the ambiguity: these devices sweep radio frequencies rapidly, stitching together fragments of broadcasts, static bursts, and interstation hiss, and the brain assembles the fragments into sentences in real time. The listener is not hearing the dead. The listener is hearing the radio, edited by expectation. Controlled tests are unambiguous: when ghost hunters are given recordings and asked to agree on what the voices say, agreement is at chance levels; when the same recordings are played backwards, new "voices" appear, equally convincing and equally meaningless; and when experimenters prime listeners with suggested content before playback, the listeners hear the suggestion. The voices live in the listener, not the tape.

The Stone Tape theory, named by Nigel Kneale's 1972 BBC television play and absorbed into paranormal folklore ever since, holds that buildings and landscapes record traumatic events — emotionally charged moments imprinted onto stone and brick like grooves on a phonograph record, replayed under the right conditions as apparitions and sounds. Its genealogy is older than its name: Charles Babbage's 1837 Ninth Bridgewater Treatise argued that every word spoken left "a permanent impression on the earth's surface," the nineteenth-century Society for Psychical Research investigated "place memories," and T.C. Lethbridge's 1961 Ghost and Ghoul proposed that powerful events left traces in the fabric of places. The theory fails on four questions that no proponent has ever answered: what is recorded, in what medium, by what mechanism, and how is it played back? Stone is not a recording medium; its crystal lattices hold no audio, no images, no event logs, and every proposed carrier — quartz piezoelectricity, iron oxide films, water memory, electromagnetic residues — has been tested and found incapable of storing the claimed information. The famous cases the theory cites have simpler explanations: the York Treasurer's House phantom of a Roman legion, investigated seriously by the SPR and attributed to the location's acoustics and the power of suggestion; the Versailles incident of 1901, in which two English schoolteachers reported encounters with Marie Antoinette's court, which archival research showed to be a confabulation assembled from guidebook details. Both sections — the EVP and the Stone Tape — are preserved here not as open anomalies but as the two clearest demonstrations in this document of how a real human experience (hearing voices in noise, feeling a presence in an old place) generates a theory to explain it, and how the theory outlives every test performed on it. The experiences are real. The tapes are blank. The stones do not remember.


## 124. The Stoned Ape Theory [FRINGE-CLAIM]

McKenna's hypothesis: psilocybin drove hominin cognitive evolution. Documented as speculation with zero fossil or genomic support; psilocybin biosynthesis evolved independently in fungi multiple times, which neither confirms nor refutes it. Its cultural influence vastly exceeds its evidence — the pattern of this entire section.

---

# PART XIV — THE PATTERNS

Synthesis is inference, labeled as such. Five patterns recur across the entire inventory:

1. **The instrumented anomalies resist hardest.** Hessdalen (43 years of data, no consensus), ball lightning (150+ theories, no killer observation), the South Atlantic Anomaly (live, growing), earthquake lights (2,000 years documented, mechanism partial), the Hum (mapped for 30 years, causes plural). Where instruments exist and consensus does not, the anomaly is real.

2. **Solutions cluster as "ordinary physics, exotic combinations."** Sailing stones (thin ice + light wind + shallow pond), the Dark Day (fire smoke + inversion), milky seas (bacteria + algae + mass expulsion), Roman concrete (hot-mixed lime clasts), the will-o'-the-wisp (phosphine + microlightning), moai walking (rocking + ropes), Devil's Kettle (immediate subsurface resurgence). The components were always known; the combination was not.

3. **The deep Earth and the deep ocean are the same anomaly: inaccessible frontier.** The mantle's blobs, the core's rotation, the transition zone's water, the hadal ecosystem, the deep biosphere, the brine pools, the CCZ's unnamed species — better maps of Mars exist than of the mantle's base or the hadal floor. Every major unsolved geophysical anomaly is a measurement problem wearing a mystery costume.

4. **Magnetism is the connective tissue.** The SAA above the African blob; geomagnetic jerks; bird and butterfly compasses; strandings correlating with geomagnetic storms (one study) and not correlating (another — both preserved); rock-stress piezoelectricity for earthquake lights; magnetotactic bacteria in animal microbiomes; magnetite chains in human brains. A field we cannot see organizes anomalies across physics, biology, and geology.

5. **The fraud file teaches as much as the anomaly file.** Cardiff Giant, N-rays, polywater, cold fusion, crystal skulls, the 2002 giant photo, Tartaria — each dissolved under examination. An anomaly's survival is inversely proportional to how well it survives being looked at directly. The residue that survives examination — quasicrystals, the coelacanth, the deep biosphere, ball lightning's soil lines, the SAA — is small, durable, and the reason the search continues.

Every entry in this document follows the same discipline: the etymology of "anomaly" — *anōmalos*, "not even" — as the organizing principle; the evidence gathered without adopting anyone's theory; pedigree tags on every claim; both sides of every genuine dispute; the boring answer stated where it is the answer; the absence of an answer stated where it is absent. What survives that discipline is the true inventory of what does not fit — the anomalies of Earth, in full.
